public_rationale: Semafor's January 27, 2023 report documents outsourced programmers creating training material for OpenAI, supporting the outsourcing component [e1]. It does not establish poor working conditions for that workforce [e1]. The Guardian's August 2, 2023 report describes workers' allegations about employment in 2021–2022, which cannot establish conditions in January 2023 [e2]. Neither item establishes the asserted historical shift from graduate-student programming to outsourced corrective work [e1, e2].
limitations: The contemporary contractor report does not establish working conditions, while the retrospective allegations concern an earlier employment period [e1, e2].
The evidence provides no matched historical comparison showing the extent of the asserted workforce transition [e1, e2].

our_interpretation: The uncertainty concerns how much AI has changed. The outsourcing assertion is affirmative, not a conditional forecast.

The plain reading is that AI companies increasingly use outsourced workers under poor conditions to supply corrective human input formerly supplied by academic programmers. It does not require every contractor to work under such conditions.
Handcrafting includes human-written training examples and corrective labels; this is an analogy, not an assertion that labeling and programming are technically identical.
For the ongoing state described as now, use January 2023, the latest complete month before publication. Earlier employment and academic work provide historical context.
criteria.support_condition: Evidence establishes contemporary outsourcing of corrective AI work under poor working conditions and documents the asserted shift from academic programming to this workforce.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Comparable historical and contemporary evidence shows that the asserted shift did not occur, or that the supposedly exploitative corrective outsourcing was materially misdescribed.
